claims.label: Table1 Stone bunds /stone lines
claims.native_quote:
Stone bunds /stone lines
A barrier built by piling stones parallel to contour lines, practiced in areas where
suﬃcient stones can be collected. About 0.3 m deep foundation and 0.75 m high (at the
downslope side) is recommended. Depending on management, stone bunds can develop
to bench terraces (series of ﬂat cultivable steps). Commonly practiced in eastern and
southern Africa, from Eritrea to Botswana, especially in moderate rainfall areas with
adequate stones.
(Mati, 2007; Reddy, 2016)

claims.label: Table1 Level or graded soil bunds
claims.native_quote:
Level or graded soil bunds
Level soil bunds built parallel to contour lines (zero gradients) by digging ditches and
mounding excavated soils. Construction involves removal of soil from a ditch (at least
0.5 m deep, 0.5 m wide), embanked at downslope of the ditch. The recommended
maximum length of soil bund is 50 m, having tied-ridges (of 0.05 m long) at 10 m
intervals in its ditch. Common in Ethiopia and other countries (e.g. Kenya, where they
are called Fanya chini, meaning throwing downslope). The term contour bunds is also
used in the literature. In southern Africa, soil bunds are labeled as earthen bunds, built
by excavating soil from both up and downslope sides of the embankment and with the
comparatively shallow channel. In Zimbabwe, they are named dead level contours. In
general, the level soil bunds are preferred if mean annual rainfall is < 1400 mm.
Graded soil bunds are constructed following similar procedures to the level soil bunds
but having a gradient of about 1% between bund and contour line. Built in high rainfall
(> 1400 mm year−1) areas with poorly draining soil and designed to discharge excess
surface runoﬀ.
Level/graded soil bunds ﬁt in well-drained and deep (> 0.5 m) soil with a slope of up to
30%. Practiced in Ethiopia, Tanzania, Kenya, and Rwanda.
(Gowing et al., 1999; Mati, 2007; WOCAT, 2011;
Mupangwa et al., 2012; Hurni et al., 2016)

claims.label: Table1 Level or graded Fanya juu
claims.native_quote:
Level or graded Fanya juu
Level Fanya juu is built parallel to contour line (zero gradients) but graded Fanya juu is
constructed with gradient of about 1% with the contour line to slowly discharge excess
water in high rainfall area. Both are built by digging a ditch (0.5 m wide, 0.6 m deep) at
downslope of an embankment. That means, the soil removed from the ditch will be
accumulated at its upslope side. Bottom width of the embankment vary (on average
about 1.3 m) with slope and soil texture, wider in coarse textured soil and steep slope.
Like soil bunds, the recommended maximum length of Fanya juu is 50 m, having tied-
ridges at 10 m intervals in the ditch. The tied-ridges in ditch avoid side ﬂow of
accumulated water. First developed in Kenya and spread to other East African
countries. Fanya juu and soil bunds require similar soil and rainfall conditions.
Downslope spacing (like soil bunds and stone bunds) depends on the steepness of the
land, far spaced on the gentle slope. Fanya juu gradually develops into a bench terrace
after which the ditch, in most cases, is removed by tillage and included in the cultivated
area.
(Mati, 2007; WOCAT, 2011; Hurni et al., 2016)

claims.label: Table1 Vegetative barriers (hedgerows,
claims.native_quote:
Vegetative barriers (hedgerows,
grass strips)
Woody plants (tree/shrub species), preferably deep rooting, legume and other species
with multiple uses (eg Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea), are planted along contour
lines as hedgerows. Within a row, plants are spaced at 0.2–0.3 m. Hedgerows develop
to terraces after some years. Organic matter input from litterfall and root exudates, and
nitrogen ﬁxation (in leguminous species) are additional gains to the soil.
Deep rooting perennial grass strips (eg vetiver) may form hedges (width 0.5–1 m),
which are eﬀective in the land with slope < 15%. Common names are grass barrier or
grass buﬀer. Grass strips are commonly practiced in Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, and
Ethiopia and progressively develop to terraces because of sediment trapping.
(Kiepe, 1995) (Banda et al., 1994; Dalton et al.,
1996; Gowing et al., 1999; Ghadiri et al., 2001)

claims.label: Table1 Trash lines
claims.native_quote:
Trash lines
Less common (practiced in Kenya and Ethiopia) and obtained by piling crop residues
and other plant materials along contour lines. Also called mulch lines. Their service
depends on the type of original material, termite attack and pressure of roaming cattle.
Dissemination of this technique is limited due to competing demand for crop residue
and trashes.
(Hughes and Venema, 2005; Giller et al., 2009;
WOCAT, 2011)

claims.label: Table1 Bench terraces
claims.native_quote:
Bench terraces
(Nearly) ﬂat cultivable steps constructed by cutting and ﬁlling soil. Alternatively,
bench terraces can progressively develop from bunds, Fanya juu and vegetative
barriers. Because of a high labor demand, constructed bench terraces are less practiced.
Depending on soil texture, crop type, and expected runoﬀ, bench terraces can be
designed to retain water or allow its slow discharge.
(Mati, 2007; Tugizimana, 2011)

claims.label: Table1 Open ridges or tied-ridge
claims.native_quote:
Open ridges or tied-ridge
Shallow depressions in which rainwater is conserved commonly in dry areas. Small
ridges, with all sides tied form a rectangular micro-basin (depressions). Dimensions of
tied-ridges vary, based on crop type, rainfall, and soil characteristics; commonly
0.2–0.3 m high, 0.8–2 m long, and spaced at 1.5–5 m distance. Eﬀective on lands with
gentle slope. Tied-ridges are sometimes labeled as furrow (plow cut) diking, or basin/
micro-basin tillage. The rainwater (falling on the ridges and in furrow) accumulate in
furrow, enrich soil moisture and beneﬁt crops planted on the ridge/in furrow. Crops are
planted in furrows (depressions) or on ridges depending on crop type, soil texture and
moisture availability. Commonly tested in Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Zambia.
(Biamah et al., 1993; Jensen et al., 2003)
(Jensen et al., 2003)
(Brhane et al., 2006)

targeting_gate.verbatim_anchor:
The estimated optimal CCR depends to a large extent on the runoff coefﬁcient
that is used in Eqs. (3) and (4). Fig. 10 shows that runoff coefﬁcients higher than 0.2
are exceptional on initially dry soils. However, according to Mtimet (1994) the
average runoff coefﬁcient of watersheds smaller than 10 km2 is 0.9, which results in a
CCR of only 1.25 considering Eq. (3) and using the rainfall and crop data of the
Amrich jessr. Chahbani (1996) proposed a maximum CCR of 3 and 5 if the average
annual precipitation is 150–250 and 100–150 mm, respectively. In case the average
annual precipitation is below 100 mm, he stated that the CCR should be lower than
10. According to Eq. (3) and taking into account the CCR values proposed by
Chahbani (1996), an average annual runoff coefﬁcient of 0.33–0.6 is needed to attain
an annual water amount of 500 mm for crop production.
The large variability in CCR mentioned in literature, reﬂects the large range of
runoff coefﬁcients that are used. Runoff generation depends on rainfall intensity and
inﬁltration rate, both of which showing a large spatial and temporal variability,
especially in arid regions with non homogeneous soils due to sealing and rock
fragments. The measured inﬁltration rates in this study correspond well with
literature values but further research is needed on different sites in order to obtain
accurate estimates of the runoff coefﬁcient and its variability.
